## Champ

### Population censuses

The data are offered to users in particular for comparing
                     municipalities, grouping variable categories or obtaining results on
                     personalized sets of municipalities.
Derived from calculations linked to sampling techniques, the
                     data in terms of numbers are provided with several decimal places; these
                     must be used for all calculations carried out, in order to avoid
                     rounding errors.
For more information on the population census, consult the page
                     of [presentation of the
                        population census](/en/information/2564729).
The data come either from the main farm (princ.) or from the
                     complementary farm (compl).
For more methodological information, you can consult the sheets ["Tips on using census results"](/en/information/2529061).
These sheets present the characteristics of the population
                     census and deal with their consequences on the use of the data.
                     They specify in particular the changes affecting the main statistical
                     variables and their comparability with previous censuses.

### Civil register

Annual statistics concerning domiciled birthsare drawn up from the statistical bulletins of civil status, drawn up by
                     the mayors, at the time and in the municipality where the births take
                     place. They relate to births having taken place in all the
                     municipalities of France. Births that took place abroad or in the
                     overseas communities (COM) are not counted.
The "commune" variable corresponds to the commune of the
                     mother's domicile in France.
The statistics include declarative judgments of birth, but do
                     not take into account stillbirths.

Annual statistics concerning domiciled deathsare drawn up from civil status statistics bulletins drawn up by the
                     mayors, at the time and in the municipality where the deaths took place.
                     They relate to deaths that have occurred in all municipalities in
                     France. Deaths having occurred abroad or in overseas communities (COM)
                     are not counted.
The "commune" variable corresponds to the commune of the
                     deceased's domicile in France.
The statistics include declarative judgments of deaths.

### Localised disposable income system (Filosofi)

The scope covers individuals belonging
                     to ordinary tax households whose disposable income is positive or zero.
The share of taxed households is calculated on the basis of
                     households whose declared income is positive or zero.

### All employees databases (BTS)

The scope covers private-sector employees,
                     including work-study students, interns, and those on subsidized employment contracts,
                     excluding agricultural workers and private employers.

### Business Demography Information System (Side)

The indicators relate to the creation and stock of companies and
                     establishments in all non-agricultural productive and market activities.
                     This field includes financial activities.
When referring to enterprises, all counts actually relate to
                     legal units for this source. When a legal unit comprises several
                     establishments, it is located at its head office.
The number of new enterprises or establishments corresponds to
                     the number of legal units or establishments created during year N.
The number of businesses or establishments in year N corresponds
                     to the number of legal units or economically active establishments in N.

### Pay and salaried employment localized file (Flores)

The Flores system (Pay and salaried employment localized file)
                     covers establishments that have employed at least one employee during
                     the year, in France excluding Mayotte.
                     In this municipal database, the data made available is also restricted
                     to establishments active at the end of the year (last week of December),
                     which excludes establishments which ceased their activity during the
                     year.
The salaried workforce at the end of the year corresponds to the
                     number of positions present in the last week of December in the
                     employing establishment.
                     The workforce at the end of the year in some establishments may
                     therefore be zero, if the employee (s) during the year were no longer
                     employed at the end of December.
Flores covers all salaried employment, regardless of the sector
                     of activity and the type of employer (public or private, including
                     individual employers).
                     Establishments under the Ministry of the Armed Forces (military
                     personnel as well as civilians) are excluded from the scope.
The Flores device succeeds Clap, whose last vintage described
                     the year 2015. The results from Flores and Clap are not comparable,
                     and therefore should not be the subject of evolving comparative
                     analyzes.
Specifically:
-Clap covered all active establishments, employers and
                     non-employers. The number of establishments with zero staff at the end
                     of the year was therefore much higher in Clap,
                     because of this difference in field.
- Conversely, Clap only counted so-called non-ancillary jobs,
                     that is to say those exceeding a certain threshold of remuneration and /
                     or duration.
                     This restriction has been removed in Flores, which counts all
                     workstations.

### Permanent database of facilities

The permanent database of facilities (BPE) is a database
                     intended for statistical purposes. It lists a wide range of facilities
                     and services, whether commercial or not, that are accessible to the
                     public throughout France as of January 1st each year.
The permanent database of facilities (BPE) is powered by
                     different sources : [sources
                        used](/en/metadonnees/source/operation/s2216/processus-statistique).

### Hotel occupancy survey

The field covers tourist hotels, classified or not, with more
                     than 5 bedrooms and campsites with more than 10 pitches, classified or
                     not,
                     including residential campsites. It also covers other collective tourist
                     accommodation.
Statistics on the accommodation offer are established in
                     conjunction with the regional tourism committees (CRT).
                     They are offered at municipal level for France (excluding Mayotte).
The statistics concerning the outdoor hotel industry relate to
                     the campsites offering sites for passing customers intended for tourists
                     not electing domicile there, as well as on campsites offering pitches
                     rented year-round, that is to say to a single customer for the entire
                     opening period of the campsite.
Classified hotels and campsites are classified according to the
                     	new classification nomenclature implemented by the operator Atout
                     	France.

### Unique electoral register

The unique electoral register covers all french territories
                     except New Caledonia.
The scope concerns voters registered on the main electoral list.
The main electoral lists, maintained by the municipalities,
                     record french voters associated with them who are eligible to
                     participate in elections governed by the provisions of the electoral
                     code, as well as any other consultations based on these lists.

## Data description
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_French_departments_by_population&action=edit&section=1)]
The figures include:
- [population without double counting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_without_double_counting) for 1999;
- municipal population (legal population in 2008, with effect from 1 January 2011)[[1]](#cite_note-pop2006-1) published in [decree No. 2010-1723 of 30 December 2010](http://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/affichTexte.do?cidTexte=JORFTEXT000023333756&dateTexte=&categorieLien=id) as amended by Decree No. 2011-343 of 28 March 2011 which corresponds to data compiled as at 1 January 2008.
- municipal population (legal population in 2019 with effect from 1 January 2022)[[2]](#cite_note-pop2019-2)
The total population takes into account double counting.

## Evolution
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_French_departments_by_population&action=edit&section=2)]
Between 1999 and 2006 all French departments had grown in population with the exception of the following seven departments: Allier and Cantal in [Auvergne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auvergne_(region)), Creuse in [Limousin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limousin), Ardennes and Haute-Marne in [Champagne-Ardenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne-Ardenne), Nièvre in [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy), and Vosges in [Lorraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorraine). See [population decline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_decline) for more information.
In contrast the seven departments that have gained the most population in absolute value are Haute-Garonne, Gironde, Bouches-du-Rhône, Seine-Saint-Denis, Loire-Atlantique, Hauts-de Seine, and Hérault.
[Guadeloupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadeloupe) has seemingly lost population between 1999 and 2008. However, this diminution of the legal population is due to the creation of the overseas communities of [Saint Barthélemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Barthélemy) and [Saint Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collectivity_of_Saint_Martin). In the 1999 census, the population of Guadeloupe without the [arrondissement of Saint-Martin-Saint-Barthélemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrondissement_of_Saint-Martin-Saint-Barthélemy) was 386,566 inhabitants. The department's population has actually increased by more than 15,000 people over the period based on a constant territory.

1. Synthesize, don't summarize. Connect, compare, and weigh across sources. Where sources converge, say so and cite the agreement [[s3]] [[s7]]. Where they diverge — different numbers, different timelines, conflicting claims — surface the disagreement explicitly with both citations. Source B says Y [[s9]].', and do not stack sourced facts and stop: a paragraph that lists what is known is not finished until it says what those facts add up to — which carries the most weight, what they settle, what they leave open. 2. Match the strength of a claim to its source. Attribute vendor claims, forecasts, disputed claims, and consequential secondary reporting that has not been verified against its original source. A product announcement is not demonstrated performance; a stated design life is not observed service life. Name the organization, author, or document when known. Unknown authorship is a reason for caution, not permission to assert a claim as fact. Honor the requested evidence standard: when primary documentation is requested, a secondary account alone does not satisfy it. Use an admitted original when its text supports the claim; otherwise narrow the claim and disclose the limitation, or omit an unreliable detail. Do not cite a primary page merely because its title matches. A summary and its original are not independent corroboration.

3. Measured, analytical register. Cut these words and any like them: 'transformative,' 'revolutionary,' 'poised to revolutionize,' 'pivotal,' 'game-changing,' 'breakthrough,' 'paradigm shift,' 'cutting-edge.' Describe, weigh, and qualify. The reader is an analyst, not a marketer.

4. Foreground tension and uncertainty. Where the field disagrees, where projected timelines slip, where the evidence is one-sided — surface it, don't smooth it over. The gap between announcements and shipping reality is often the finding. Tensions go in the body, not in footnotes.

5. Stay grounded. Every factual claim — including list items, table cells, and callouts — carries its [[id]] citation, placed right after the claim it supports: a sentence that joins two facts from two sources carries a citation after each ('the U.S. fleet passed 26 GW in 2024 [[s1]] and added 57.6 GWh in 2025 [[s40]]'), and reads as one sentence, not as two list entries. One citation per claim is the norm: the source the claim rests on. Several belong only on a sentence that itself compares those sources or reports their agreement; a chain of ids after a plain statement of fact is not support, it is noise the reader has to step over. An inference that goes beyond what any single source says is written so the reader can tell it is yours — in your own words, not a stock opening phrase repeated through the report — and cites the sources it is drawn from. Evidence of one example establishes at least one, not the only example or a global total. Preserve dates, populations, product versions, and applicability conditions. Shared terminology or simultaneous activity does not establish causation. Do not reverse a dependency or turn a conditional possibility into a certainty. Do not turn missing coverage into a finding of absence. Do not narrate tool use or internal checks; that style rule never requires concealing uncertainty. **Paris is the capital of France, and its city-proper population is roughly 2.0–2.1 million people.** The capital status is confirmed independently by Wikipedia, the UNECE statistical database, and the France Wikipedia entry [[s2]] [[s5]] [[s8]]. For population, the authoritative INSEE 2023 census puts the Paris commune at 2,103,778 [[s1]] [[s6]], while INSEE's provisional estimate for 1 January 2026 is 2,047,600 [[s3]] — the difference reflects a documented ongoing decline of about 0.6–0.9% per year, not a contradiction. At wider scales, the Île-de-France region holds about 12.6 million people as of 1 January 2026 [[s3]], and the Paris metropolitan area about 13.3 million (2023) [[s2]].

## Capital status

Multiple independent sources agree that Paris is France's capital. The Wikipedia article on Paris is framed explicitly as being about the "Capital of France," and its administration section states that as the capital, Paris hosts the seat of national government: the President at the Élysée Palace, the Prime Minister at Hôtel Matignon, and both houses of Parliament (the Senate in the Palais du Luxembourg and the National Assembly in the Palais Bourbon) [[s2]]. The UNECE statistical database lists France's capital as "Paris" in its country profile [[s5]], and the France Wikipedia entry identifies Paris as the country's "capital and largest city" [[s8]]. The Île-de-France Wikipedia article likewise describes the region as "containing the capital city of France, Paris" [[s9]]. There is no disagreement among sources on this point.

## Population of Paris city proper

The best-anchored figure for the city itself comes from INSEE, France's national statistics office. The 2023 census gives the Paris commune a municipal population of 2,103,778, with a density of about 19,960 inhabitants per km² [[s1]]. These figures are the official "populations de référence" for 2023, authenticated by decree and in force from 1 January 2026 [[s6]]. INSEE's provisional estimate for 1 January 2026 is lower, at 2,047,600, with the Paris department losing roughly 18,000 residents during 2025 [[s3]]. Wikipedia's infobox carries the same January 2026 estimate of 2,047,602 [[s2]].

The gap between the 2023 census figure and the 2026 estimate is consistent with a long-running decline rather than a data conflict: INSEE records an average annual population change of −0.6% between 2017 and 2023, driven by a negative migration balance (−1.2%/yr) that outweighs a positive natural balance (+0.5%/yr) [[s1]]. Wikipedia reports the city lost 122,919 residents (about 5%) between 2013 and 2023 [[s2]]. The historical series shows this is a long-term pattern: the commune peaked at 2,590,771 in 1968 and has fallen to 2,103,778 in 2023 [[s6]] [[s7]], and is well below the historical peak of about 2.9 million in 1921 [[s2]].

| Île-de-France region | 12,594,500 | 1 Jan 2026 | [[s3]] |
| Paris metropolitan area | 13,320,752 | 2023 | [[s2]] |
| France (total) | 68,776,000 | 2024 | [[s5]] |

## Wider scales: region and metro area

Which population is "the population of Paris" depends on the geographic scope, and the evidence supports a clear ordering. The Île-de-France region — often called the Paris Region — was estimated at 12,594,500 inhabitants on 1 January 2026, growing 0.36% in 2025, though Paris itself was the only department losing population [[s3]]. An earlier official estimate put the region at 12,271,794 on 1 January 2023 [[s9]]. The Paris metropolitan area (aire d'attraction) was 13,320,752 in 2023 per INSEE data cited by Wikipedia [[s2]], and the France Wikipedia article describes a metropolitan population of over 13 million [[s8]]. An intermediate scope, the Métropole du Grand Paris (Paris plus inner-suburb departments and airport communes, 814 km²), had 6.945 million residents in 2015 — a useful benchmark, though the figure is dated [[s2]].

For national context, France's total population was 68,776,000 in 2024 per UNECE [[s5]], with a January 2026 estimate of about 69.08 million including overseas France [[s8]]. On these figures, the city of Paris holds roughly 3% of the national population and the Île-de-France region roughly 18–19%.

## Limits of the evidence

The figures above are well-sourced but carry conditions worth stating plainly. The 2023 census figure (2,103,778) is the official authenticated number, while the 1 January 2026 figures are provisional estimates that INSEE revises — the Île-de-France population for 1 January 2025 was itself revised upward from 12,450,900 to 12,549,300 between publications [[s3]]. One attempted cross-check (citypopulation.de) returned only a bot-check page and contributed no data [[s4]]. A Wikipedia list of French departments carries an explicit out-of-date-information notice and reports an older 2019 legal population for the Paris department (2,165,423) [[s11]]; it is consistent with the decline trend but superseded by the INSEE census figures. No source in the evidence pool provides a more recent official figure than the provisional 2026 estimates, so the "current" population is best stated as approximately 2.0–2.1 million for the city proper, with the exact value depending on the reference date.

## Conclusion

The answer is settled on both parts. Paris is the capital of France, where the President, Prime Minister, and both parliamentary houses sit [[s2]] [[s5]] [[s8]]. Its population is roughly 2.0–2.1 million within the city limits: 2,103,778 per the official 2023 census [[s1]] [[s6]], trending down to a provisional 2,047,600 at the start of 2026 [[s3]]. Readers should match the scope to their purpose — about 2 million for the city, about 7 million for the Greater Paris metropolis (2015 figure) [[s2]], and about 12.6 million for the Île-de-France region [[s3]] — and note that the city's population has been declining for decades while the wider region continues to grow [[s1]] [[s3]].

Paris[[b]](#cite_note-8) is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city) and [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_communes_in_France_with_over_20,000_inhabitants) of [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France), with an estimated city population of 2.04 million in an area of 105.4 km2 (40.7 sq mi), as of January 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paris&action=edit),[[4]](#cite_note-Pop.Paris-5) and a metropolitan population of 13.3 million (2023). Located on the [Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine) in the centre of the [Île-de-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île-de-France) region, it is the [largest metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_Europe) and [fourth-most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_the_European_Union_by_population_within_city_limits) in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union) (EU). Paris is nicknamed the "City of Light" mainly due to its leading role in the [Age of Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment).
Administratively, Paris is divided into [twenty arrondissements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrondissements_of_Paris) (districts), each having their own cultural identity. [Haussmann's renovation of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haussmann's_renovation_of_Paris), which created new boulevards, parks, and public works, gave birth to a modern city known as the "[capital of the 19th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris,_Capital_of_the_19th_Century)". Paris is a major railway, motorway, and air-transport hub; in 2024 [Charles de Gaulle Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle_Airport) was the EU's [busiest airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe). Paris has one of the most [sustainable transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_transportation) systems in the world and is one of only two cities that have received the [Sustainable Transport Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_Transport_Award) twice. Its [Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau)-decorated [Métro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Métro) has become a symbol of the city. Paris is known for its museums and architectural landmarks: the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre) is the largest and most-visited museum in the world; the [Musée d'Orsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_d'Orsay), [Musée Marmottan Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_Marmottan_Monet), and [Musée de l'Orangerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_de_l'Orangerie) are noted for their collections of French [Impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism) art, while the [Musée National d'Art Moderne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_National_d'Art_Moderne), [Musée Rodin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_Rodin), and [Musée Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_Picasso) are noted for their collections of [modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_art) and [contemporary art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_art). Parts of the city along the Seine have been designated a [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO) [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site) since 1991[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paris&action=edit).
The [president of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France) and both houses of the [French Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Parliament) sit in Paris. By the end of the [Western Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire), the town was known as Parisius, a [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language) name that later became Paris in French.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeunier201412-21) [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity) was introduced in the middle of the 3rd century AD by Saint [Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Denis_of_Paris), the first Bishop of Paris: according to legend, when he refused to renounce his faith before the Roman occupiers, he was beheaded on the hill which became known as Mons Martyrum (Latin "Hill of Martyrs"), later "[Montmartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montmartre)", from where he walked headless to the north of the city; the place where he fell and was buried became an important religious shrine, the [Basilica of Saint-Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_of_Saint-Denis), and many French kings are buried there.[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt2009210–211-22)The [Wall of Philippe Auguste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_of_Philip_II_Augustus), oldest city wall in Paris
[Clovis the Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I), the first king of the [Merovingian dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merovingian_dynasty), made the city his capital from 508.[[21]](#cite_note-23) As the Frankish domination of Gaul began, there was a gradual immigration by the [Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks) to Paris, and the Parisian [Francien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francien_language) dialects were born. Fortification of the [Île de la Cité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île_de_la_Cité) failed to avert [sacking by Vikings in 845](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Paris_(845)). Still, Paris's strategic importance—with its bridges preventing ships from passing—was established by successful defence in the [Siege of Paris (885–886)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Paris_(885–886)), for which the then [Count of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Paris) (comte de Paris), [Odo of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odo_of_France), was elected king of [West Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Francia).[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones199448-24) From the [Capetian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Capet) dynasty that began with the 987 election of [Hugh Capet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Capet), [Count of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Paris) and [Duke of the Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_the_Franks) (duc des Francs), as king of a unified [West Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Francia), Paris gradually became the largest and most prosperous city in France.[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt2009210–211-22)

### High and Late Middle Ages to Louis XIV

See also: [Paris in the Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_Middle_Ages), [Paris in the 16th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_16th_century), and [Paris in the 17th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_17th_century)The [Palais de la Cité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_de_la_Cité) and [Sainte-Chapelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Chapelle), viewed from the Left Bank, from the [Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Très_Riches_Heures_du_duc_de_Berry), June 1410
By the end of the 12th century, Paris had become the political, economic, religious, and cultural capital of France.[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201027-25) [Maurice de Sully](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_de_Sully), bishop of Paris, started the construction of the [Notre Dame Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_de_Paris) in 1163, and was completed after 182 years.[[24]](#cite_note-26) After the marshland between the river Seine and its slower 'dead arm' to its north was filled in[[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify)] from around the 10th century,[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBussmann198522-27) Paris's cultural centre began to move to the Right Bank. In 1137, a new city marketplace (today's [Les Halles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Halles)) replaced the two smaller ones on the Île de la Cité and [Place de Grève (Place de l'Hôtel de Ville)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_de_l'Hôtel-de-Ville_–_Esplanade_de_la_Libération).[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_VitriacoHinnebusch1972262-28) The latter location housed the headquarters of Paris's river trade corporation. This organisation later became, unofficially (although formally in later years), Paris's first municipal government.
In the late 12th century, [Philip Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_France) extended the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre) fortress to defend the city against river invasions from the west, gave the city its first walls between 1190 and 1215, rebuilt its bridges to either side of its central island, and paved its main thoroughfares.[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarmant201236–40-29) In 1190, he transformed Paris's former cathedral school into a student-teacher corporation that became the [University of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris) and drew students from all of Europe.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarmant201228–29-30)[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201027-25)
With 200,000 inhabitants in 1328, Paris, then already the capital of France, was the most populous city of Europe. By comparison, London in 1300 had 80,000 inhabitants.[[29]](#cite_note-ParisDigest-31) Around 1340 the city had between 250,000 and 300,000 inhabitants.[[30]](#cite_note-32) By the early fourteenth century, so much filth had collected inside urban Europe that French and Italian cities were naming streets after human waste. In medieval Paris, several street names were inspired by merde, the French word for "shit".[[31]](#cite_note-33)The [Hôtel de Sens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hôtel_de_Sens) (c. 15th–16th), former residence of the Archbishop of Sens
During the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War), Paris was occupied by England-friendly [Burgundian forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundian_State) from [1418](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_coup_d'état_and_massacres_of_1418), before being occupied outright by the English when [Henry V of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England) entered the French capital in 1420;[[32]](#cite_note-34) despite a 1429 effort by [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc) to liberate the city,[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro199652–53-35) it would remain under English occupation until 1436.

## Administration

Main article: [Administration of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_of_Paris)

### City government

Further information: [Arrondissements of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrondissements_of_Paris)
See also: [Mayor of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Paris)A map of the [arrondissements of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrondissements_of_Paris)
For almost all of its long history, except for a few brief periods, Paris was governed directly by representatives of the king, emperor, or president of France. In 1974, Paris was granted municipal autonomy by the National Assembly.[[109]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996334-112) The first modern elected mayor of Paris was [Jacques Chirac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Chirac), elected in March 1977, becoming the city's first mayor since 1871 and only the fourth since 1794. The current mayor is [Emmanuel Grégoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Grégoire), a member of the [Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_(France)), who was elected in [2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Paris_municipal_election).[[110]](#cite_note-113)The [Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hôtel_de_Ville,_Paris), or city hall
The mayor of Paris is [elected indirectly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indirect_election) by Paris voters. The voters of each of the city's 20 arrondissements elect members to the [Conseil de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_de_Paris) (Council of Paris), which elects the mayor. The council is composed of 163 members. Each arrondissement is allocated many seats, dependent upon its population, from 10 members for each of the least-populated arrondissements to 34 members for the most populated. The council is elected using [closed list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_list) [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation) in a [two-round system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-round_system).[[111]](#cite_note-Election_Code_–_Article_L260-114)
Party lists winning an absolute [majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority) in the first round – or at least a [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_(voting)) in the second round – automatically win half the seats of an arrondissement. The remaining half of the seats are distributed proportionally to all lists which win at least 5% of the vote, using the [highest averages method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highest_averages_method).[[111]](#cite_note-Election_Code_–_Article_L260-114) This ensures that the winning party or coalition always wins a majority of the seats, even if they do not win an absolute majority of the vote.[[112]](#cite_note-Pariscouncil-115)
Before the [2020 Paris municipal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Paris_municipal_election), each of Paris's 20 arrondissements had its own town hall and a directly elected council ([conseil d'arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_d'arrondissement)), which elects an arrondissement mayor.[[113]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShales200716-116) The council of each arrondissement is composed of members of the Conseil de Paris, and members who serve only on the council of the arrondissement. The number of deputy mayors in each arrondissement varies depending on its population. As of 1996, there were 20 arrondissement mayors and 120 deputy mayors.[[109]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996334-112) The creation of [Paris Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Centre), a unified administrative division with a single mayor covering the first four arrondissements, took effect with the said 2020 election. The other 16 arrondissements continue to have their own mayors.[[114]](#cite_note-117)

### Métropole du Grand Paris
A map of the Greater Paris Metropolis and its governing territories
In January 2016, the [Métropole du Grand Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Paris) came into existence.[[115]](#cite_note-MGP-118) It is an administrative structure for co-operation between the City of Paris and its nearest suburbs. It includes the City of Paris, plus the communes of the three departments of the inner suburbs, [Hauts-de-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauts-de-Seine), [Seine-Saint-Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine-Saint-Denis) and [Val-de-Marne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val-de-Marne), plus seven communes in the outer suburbs, including [Argenteuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argenteuil) in [Val d'Oise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_d'Oise) and [Paray-Vieille-Poste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paray-Vieille-Poste) in [Essonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essonne), which were added to include the major airports of Paris. The Metropole covers 814 km2 (314 sq mi). In 2015, it had a population of 6.945 million people.[[116]](#cite_note-119)[[117]](#cite_note-lemoniteur1-120)
The new structure is administered by a Metropolitan Council of 210 members, not directly elected, but chosen by the councils of the member Communes. By 2020, its basic competencies will include urban planning, housing, and protection of the environment.[[115]](#cite_note-MGP-118)[[117]](#cite_note-lemoniteur1-120) In January 2016, [Patrick Ollier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Ollier) was elected the first president of the metropolitan council. Though the Metropole has a population of nearly seven million people and accounts for 25 percent of the GDP of France, it has a very small budget: just 65 million Euros, compared with eight billion Euros for the City of Paris.[[118]](#cite_note-121)

### Regional government

The [Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region) of [Île de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île_de_France), including Paris and its surrounding communities, is governed by the [Regional Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Council_of_Île-de-France), composed of 209 members representing the different communes. In December 2015, a list of candidates of the Union of the Right, a coalition of centrist and right-wing parties, led by [Valérie Pécresse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valérie_Pécresse), narrowly won the regional election, defeating a coalition of Socialists and ecologists. The Socialists had governed the region for seventeen years. The regional council has 121 members from the Union of the Right, 66 from the Union of the Left and 22 from the extreme right National Front.[[119]](#cite_note-122)

### National government
The [Élysée Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Élysée_Palace), official residence of the [President of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France)
As the capital of France, Paris is the seat of France's [national government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_France). For the executive, the two chief officers each have their own official residences, which also serve as their offices. The [President of the French Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France) resides at the [Élysée Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Élysée_Palace).[[120]](#cite_note-123) The [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_France)'s seat is at the [Hôtel Matignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hôtel_Matignon).[[121]](#cite_note-124)[[122]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnappWright200693–94-125) Government ministries are located in various parts of the city, many near the Hôtel Matignon.[[123]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorrus2012288-126)
Both houses of the [French Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Parliament) are located on the Rive Gauche. The upper house, the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_(France)), meets in the [Palais du Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_du_Luxembourg). The more important lower house, the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(France)), meets in the [Palais Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Bourbon). The [President of the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Senate_of_France), the second-highest public official in France, with the President of the Republic being the sole superior, resides in the [Petit Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petit_Luxembourg), a smaller palace annexe to the Palais du Luxembourg.[[124]](#cite_note-127)The Palais-Royal, residence of the [Conseil d'État](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_d'État_(France))
France's highest courts are located in Paris. The [Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Cassation_(France)), the highest court in the judicial order, which reviews criminal and civil cases, is located in the [Palais de Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_de_Justice,_Paris) on the Île de la Cité.[[125]](#cite_note-128) The [Conseil d'État](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_State_(France)), which provides legal advice to the executive and acts as the highest court in the administrative order, judging litigation against public bodies, is located in the [Palais-Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais-Royal) in the [1st arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_arrondissement_of_Paris).[[126]](#cite_note-129) The [Constitutional Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Council_of_France), an advisory body with ultimate authority on the constitutionality of laws and government decrees, meets in the Montpensier wing of the Palais Royal.[[127]](#cite_note-130)

The population of the City of Paris was 2,102,650 in January 2023, down from 2,165,423 in January 2022. Between 2013 and 2023, the population fell by 122,919, or about five percent. The Mayor of Paris, [Anne Hidalgo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Hidalgo), declared that this illustrated the "de-densification" of the city, creating more green space and less crowding.[[152]](#cite_note-155)[[153]](#cite_note-156) Despite the drop, Paris remains the most densely populated city in Europe, with 252 residents per hectare, not counting parks.[[154]](#cite_note-Le_Monde,_22_January_2019-157) This drop was attributed partly to a lower birth rate, the departure of middle-class residents, and the possible loss of housing in Paris, due to short-term rentals for tourism.[[155]](#cite_note-158)
Paris is the fourth largest municipality in the European Union, after [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin), [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid) and [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome), and is the [34th most densely populated city in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_proper_by_population_density) as of 2020[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paris&action=edit).[[156]](#cite_note-worldatlas-pop-159) [Eurostat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurostat) places Paris (6.5 million people) behind London (8 million) and ahead of Berlin (3.5 million), based on the 2012 populations of what Eurostat calls "urban audit core cities".[[157]](#cite_note-160)
The population of Paris today is lower than its historical peak of 2.9 million in 1921.[[158]](#cite_note-161) The principal reasons are a significant decline in household size and a dramatic migration of residents to the suburbs between 1962 and 1975. Factors in the migration included [de-industrialisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De-industrialisation), high rent, the [gentrification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentrification) of many inner quarters, the transformation of living space into offices, and greater affluence among working families. Paris's population loss came to a temporary halt at the beginning of the 21st century. The population increased from 2,125,246 in 1999 to 2,240,621 in 2012, before declining again between 2012 and 2023.[[159]](#cite_note-162)[[160]](#cite_note-pophis-163)
Paris is the core of a built-up area that extends well beyond its limits: commonly referred to as the agglomération Parisienne, and statistically as a [unité urbaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unité_urbaine) (a measure of [urban area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area)), the Paris agglomeration's population of 11,013,774 in 2023 made it the [largest urban area in the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_urban_areas_in_the_European_Union).[[3]](#cite_note-Comparateur_de_territoires.INSEE-4) City-influenced commuter activity reaches further, in a statistical [aire d'attraction de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Metropolitan_Area), ("functional area", a statistical method comparable to a [metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area)),[[161]](#cite_note-FU-164) that had a population of 13,320,752 in 2023,[[3]](#cite_note-Comparateur_de_territoires.INSEE-4) 19.6% of the population of France,[[162]](#cite_note-165) and the [largest metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_Europe) in the [Eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone).[[163]](#cite_note-urbaneurope-166)
In 2012, the Commune of Paris was the most densely populated city in the European Union. There were 21,616 people per square kilometre within the city limits, the NUTS-3 statistical area, ahead of Inner London West, which had 10,374 people per square kilometre. In the same census, three departments bordering Paris, [Hauts-de-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauts-de-Seine), [Seine-Saint-Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine-Saint-Denis) and [Val-de-Marne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val-de-Marne), had population densities of over 10,000 people per square kilometre, ranking among the 10 most densely populated areas of the EU.[[164]](#cite_note-167)[[verification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability)]

### Migration

Under French law, people born in foreign countries with no French citizenship at birth are defined as immigrants. In the 2012 census, 135,853 residents of the City of Paris were immigrants from [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe), 112,369 were immigrants from the [Maghreb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maghreb), 70,852 from [sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa) and [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt), 5,059 from [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey), 91,297 from [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia) outside Turkey, 38,858 from the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas), and 1,365 from the [South Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania).[[165]](#cite_note-168)
In the Paris Region, 590,504 residents were immigrants from Europe, 627,078 were immigrants from the Maghreb, 435,339 from sub-Saharan Africa and Egypt, 69,338 from Turkey, 322,330 from Asia outside Turkey, 113,363 from the Americas, and 2,261 from the South Pacific.[[166]](#cite_note-169)
In 2012, there were 8,810 British citizens and 10,019 United States citizens living in the City of Paris (Ville de Paris), and 20,466 British citizens and 16,408 United States citizens living in the entire Paris Region ([Île-de-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île-de-France)).[[167]](#cite_note-170)[[168]](#cite_note-171)
In 2020–2021, about 6 million people, or 41% of the population of the Paris Region, were either immigrants (21%) or had at least one immigrant parent (20%). These figures do not include French people born in Overseas France and their direct descendants.[[169]](#cite_note-172)

#
Insee Flash Ile-de-France ·
               Avril 2026 · n° 111L’Île-de-France conserve un solde naturel largement excédentaire Bilan démographique 2025

François Dubujet (Insee)

Au 1er janvier 2026, l’Île-de-France compte 12,59 millions d’habitants. Avec 148 300 naissances
               en 2025, la baisse de la natalité se poursuit dans la région et elle est plus marquée
               qu’au niveau national. Le nombre de décès est stable en 2025, à 79 300. Bien que toujours
               largement positif, l’excédent naturel francilien se réduit à nouveau (+69 000), prolongeant
               ainsi la tendance entamée en 2015. Il demeure néanmoins le moteur de la croissance
               démographique francilienne et l’Île-de-France est, avec Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, l’une
               des deux seules régions métropolitaines conservant un excédent naturel.
Contrairement aux années précédentes, la fécondité recule autant en Île-de-France
               que dans le reste de la France, avec un indicateur conjoncturel de fécondité à 1,63
               contre 1,56 au niveau national.
L’espérance de vie à la naissance progresse à nouveau en 2025 (+0,1 an) : elle atteint
               86,5 ans pour les femmes et 82,0 ans pour les hommes.

## 12,59 millions d’habitants au 1er janvier 2026

Au 1er janvier 2026, la population de l’Île-de-France est estimée à 12 594 500 habitants
                     ([figure 1](#figure1)). Au cours de l’année 2025, la population augmente de 45 200 habitants, soit une
                     progression de 0,36 %. Cette hausse est un peu inférieure à la moyenne annuelle constatée
                     au cours des cinq dernières années (+0,45 %).
Au cours de l’année 2025, la population progresse dans tous les départements de la
                     région, à l’exception de Paris (-18 000 habitants) qui perd régulièrement des habitants
                     depuis 2012. Comme les trois années précédentes, les hausses de population sont les
                     plus fortes en Seine-Saint-Denis et en Seine-et-Marne (respectivement +13 900 et +11 200
                     habitants).

## La croissance francilienne toujours portée par l’excédent naturel

La croissance de la population francilienne est entièrement portée par le solde naturel. Toutefois, compte tenu de la baisse du nombre de naissances et du maintien du nombre
                     de décès en 2025 par rapport à 2024, l’excédent naturel régional recule légèrement
                     mais reste largement positif, passant de 73 200 habitants en 2024 à 69 000 en 2025
                     ([figure 2](#figure2)). Quant au déficit migratoire, il reste important, mais s’amenuise (de -31 400 en 2024 à -23 800 en 2025). La réduction
                     simultanée de l’excédent naturel et du déficit migratoire explique le maintien de
                     la croissance démographique dans la région.
L’Île-de-France est, avec la région Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, l’une des deux régions métropolitaines
                     où le solde naturel est positif en 2025. Néanmoins, celui d’Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes est
                     bien plus faible qu’en Île-de-France. En comparaison, le solde naturel devient négatif
                     dans les Hauts-de-France et le déficit naturel se creuse dans toutes les autres régions
                     de France métropolitaine.
En 2025, 148 300 bébés sont nés en Île-de-France, soit 4 250 de moins qu’en 2024 (-2,8 %).
                     Ce recul s’inscrit dans une baisse tandancielle. L’année 2025 est la onzième année
                     consécutive de réduction du nombre de naissances dans la région, et cette baisse est
                     plus prononcée que celle de 2024 (-1,0 %). Contrairement aux deux années précédentes,
                     elle est aussi un peu plus marquée en Île-de-France qu’en moyenne sur l’ensemble du
                     territoire national (-2,4 % en 2025). Depuis le point haut atteint en 2010, le recul
                     des naissances atteint 19,6 %, soit à peine moins que celui enregistré au niveau national
                     (-23,8 %).
La baisse continue des naissances se traduit par une diminution de la population des
                     jeunes enfants, phénomène accentué par un solde migratoire négatif à ces âges. Ainsi,
                     au 1er janvier 2026, les personnes de moins de 20 ans représentent 23,7 % de la population,
                     contre 25,3 % en 2021. À l’inverse, en haut de la pyramide des âges, le vieillissement
                     des baby-boomers accroît la proportion des seniors, qui atteint 16,7 % (contre 15,4 %
                     en 2020). De ce fait, l’indice de jeunesse, représentant le nombre de personnes de
                     moins de 20 ans pour 100 personnes de 65 ans ou plus, continue de diminuer fortement,
                     passant de 205 en 2010 à 166 en 2020 et 142 en 2026. Néanmoins, une baisse est enregistrée
                     également dans les autres régions de France métropolitaine, de sorte que le ratio
                     francilien reste le plus élevé.

## La fécondité recule autant en Île-de-France qu’au niveau national

En 2025, en Île-de-France, l’indicateur conjoncturel de fécondité (ICF) s’établit à 1,63 enfant par femme, un niveau inférieur à celui observé en 2024
                     (1,68). La baisse de l’ICF s’amplifie : elle était plus modérée l’année précédente,
                     passant de 1,71 en 2023 à 1,68 en 2024. L’ICF régional atteint ainsi un niveau historiquement
                     bas, inférieur aux niveaux faibles atteints en 1976 (1,72) et en 1994 (1,74), et s’éloigne
                     encore un peu plus du seuil de renouvellement des générations (2,05 enfants par femme). Le niveau de fécondité demeure toutefois relativement élevé
                     en Île-de-France au regard du niveau national, qui recule à 1,56 en 2025. L’écart
                     entre l’indicateur régional et l’indicateur national se maintient, traduisant une
                     baisse similaire à la moyenne nationale alors que, les années précédentes, l’Île-de-France
                     résistait un peu mieux au recul de la fécondité que la plupart des autres régions
                     métropolitaines.
L’évolution du nombre de naissances dépend à la fois du nombre de femmes en âge de
                     procréer et de leur fécondité. La population féminine de 20 à 40 ans, âges où les
                     femmes sont les plus fécondes, progresse lentement depuis 2020 pour retrouver son
                     niveau du début des années 1990. Le recul du nombre des naissances en Île-de-France
                     au cours des six dernières années s’explique donc uniquement par celui de la fécondité,
                     c’est-à-dire du nombre d’enfants par femme.
En 2025, l’ICF est une nouvelle fois au-dessous du seuil de renouvellement des générations
                     dans tous les départements de l’Île-de-France. Il se maintient à un niveau encore
                     élevé dans le Val-d’Oise (1,94) et en Seine-Saint-Denis (1,92). À Paris, le niveau
                     de l’ICF (1,26) reste l’un des plus bas des départements de France métropolitaine,
                     seulement supérieur à celui observé dans les deux départements corses (1,13). Cela
                     tient notamment à une maternité nettement plus tardive que dans les autres départements.
                     Depuis 2020, l’ICF des femmes parisiennes âgées de 35 à 49 ans est supérieur à celui
                     de celles âgées de 25 à 34 ans (respectivement 0,65 et 0,56 en 2025). Même si le recul
                     de l’âge à la maternité est une tendance générale, l’ICF des femmes de 35 à 49 ans
                     reste inférieur à celui des femmes de 25 à 34 ans, dans les autres départements franciliens
                     et au niveau régional (respectivement 0,58 et 0,93 en 2025).
Ainsi, en 2025, l’âge conjoncturel moyen à l’accouchement est de 34,6 ans à Paris, le plus élevé de la région. En Île-de-France, cet âge moyen
                     s’établit à 32,5 ans, soit un an de plus qu’en 2015 et cinq ans de plus qu’en 1981.
                     C’est le niveau le plus élevé de toutes les régions de France métropolitaine (31,2 ans
                     en moyenne).

## Une stabilité des décès et une reprise des gains d’espérance de vie

En 2025, 79 300 personnes sont décédées en Île-de-France, soit un nombre équivalent
                     à celui de 2024 (79 400). Cette relative stagnation est une caractéristique commune
                     avec la Nouvelle-Aquitaine, tandis que le nombre de décès augmente dans toutes les
                     autres régions et en France métropolitaine (+1,0 %).
Au sein de la région, l’évolution de la mortalité est très variable d’un département
                     à l’autre. Le nombre de décès diminue à Paris, en petite couronne et dans l’Essonne,
                     mais augmente dans les trois autres départements de grande couronne.
Le vieillissement de la population, avec une part croissante de personnes atteignant
                     les âges où la mortalité est plus élevée, touche tous les départements d’Île-de-France
                     comme l’ensemble de la France. À Paris, la part de la population âgée d’au moins 80 ans
                     atteint 5,3 %, un point de plus que la moyenne régionale. Ce vieillissement de la
                     population concourt à accroître la mortalité. Néanmoins, en 2025, l’Île-de-France
                     restant une région relativement jeune, le taux de mortalité y est inférieur de 3 points
                     au taux national (6,3 ‰ contre 9,4 ‰), un écart qui tend à augmenter depuis 30 ans :
                     il n’était que de 1,7 point en 1992 (7,2 ‰ contre 8,9 ‰).
En 2025, en Île-de-France, l’espérance de vie à la naissance est de 86,5 ans pour les femmes (85,9 ans pour la France entière) et de 82,0 ans
                     pour les hommes (80,3 ans au niveau national). Qu’il s’agisse des femmes ou des hommes,
                     le gain d’espérance de vie en 2025 est faible (+0,1 an), en comparaison de l’année
                     2023 où elle avait fortement augmenté par rapport aux trois années précédentes marquées
                     par une forte mortalité liée à l’épidémie de Covid-19. En revanche, ce gain est proche
                     du rythme moyen observé sur la période de 2010 à 2019, soit +0,1 an pour les femmes
                     et +0,2 an pour les hommes.

Le recensement de la population sert de base aux [estimations annuelles de population](https://www.insee.fr/fr/metadonnees/source/serie/s1169). Pour les années 2024 et suivantes, les estimations de population sont provisoires :
                        la population du recensement 2023 est actualisée au moyen d’estimations du solde naturel
                        établi à partir des statistiques d’état civil à fin novembre 2025 et du solde migratoire apparent. La population francilienne au
                        1er janvier 2025, estimée fin 2024 à 12 450 900 habitants, a ainsi été révisée fin 2025
                        à 12 549 300 habitants.

## Définitions

Le solde naturel est la différence entre le nombre de naissances et le nombre de décès enregistrés
                           au cours d’une période. S’il est positif, il s’agit d’un excédent naturel, s’il est
                           négatif, d’un déficit naturel.

Le solde migratoire est mesuré indirectement par différence entre, d’une part, l’évolution du niveau
                           de la population entre deux années successives et, d’autre part, le solde naturel.

L’indicateur conjoncturel de fécondité (ICF) est la somme des taux de fécondité par âge observés pour une année donnée.
                           Il peut être interprété comme le nombre moyen d’enfants qu’aurait une génération fictive
                           de femmes qui connaîtraient, tout au long de leur vie féconde, les taux de fécondité
                           par âge observés cette année-là. Il est exprimé en nombre d’enfants par femme. C’est
                           un indicateur synthétique des taux de fécondité par âge de l’année considérée.

Le seuil de renouvellement des générations correspond au nombre moyen d’enfants par femme nécessaire pour que chaque génération
                           en engendre une suivante de même effectif. Il est fixé à 2,05 enfants par femme, parce
                           que pour 100 filles, il naît 105 garçons.

L’âge conjoncturel moyen à l’accouchement est un âge calculé pour une génération fictive de femmes qui auraient à chaque âge
                           la fécondité observée pour les femmes du même âge l’année considérée.

L’espérance de vie à la naissance est égale à la durée de vie moyenne d’une génération fictive qui connaîtrait tout
                           au long de son existence les conditions de mortalité par âge de l’année considérée.
                           C’est un indicateur synthétique des taux de mortalité par âge de l’année considérée.

France,[[i]](#cite_note-19) officially the French Republic,[[j]](#cite_note-20) is a country primarily located in [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe).[[k]](#cite_note-21) [Its overseas regions and territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overseas_France) include [French Guiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Guiana) in [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America), [Saint Pierre and Miquelon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Pierre_and_Miquelon) in the [North Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic), the [French West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_West_Indies), and [many islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_France) in [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania) and the [Indian Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean). [Metropolitan France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_France) shares borders with [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium) and [Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxembourg) to the north; [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany) to the northeast; [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland) to the east; [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy) and [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco) to the southeast; [Andorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andorra) and [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain) to the south; and a maritime border with the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom) to the northwest. Its metropolitan area extends from the [Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine) to the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean) and from the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea) to the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel) and the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea). Its 18 [integral regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_France#List_of_administrative_regions)—five of which are overseas—span a combined area of 632,702 km2 (244,288 sq mi), with [a total population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_France) estimated at over 69.1 million in 2026. Its capital, [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_communes_in_France_with_over_20,000_inhabitants) and main cultural and economic centre is [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris), with a metropolitan population of over 13 million.
Metropolitan France was settled during the [Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age) by [Celtic tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ancient_Celtic_peoples_and_tribes) known as [Gauls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauls) before [Rome annexed the area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Gaul) in 51 BC, leading to a distinct [Gallo-Roman culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallo-Roman_culture). In the [Early Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Middle_Ages), the [Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks) formed the kingdom of [Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francia), which became the heartland of the [Carolingian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Empire). The [Treaty of Verdun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun) of 843 partitioned the empire, with [West Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Francia) evolving into the [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France). In the [High Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Middle_Ages), France was a powerful but decentralised [feudal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism) kingdom, but after [Philip II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_France) defeated the [Angevin Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angevin_Empire) and won the [Battle of Bouvines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bouvines), it became more centralized and became the most powerful country in Europe. From the mid-14th to the mid-15th centuries, France was plunged into a dynastic conflict with [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England) known as the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War). In the 16th century, [French culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_France) flourished during the [French Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Renaissance), and a [French colonial empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire) emerged. Internally, France was dominated by the conflict with the [House of Habsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Habsburg) and the [French Wars of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion) between [Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholics) and [Huguenots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenots). France was successful in the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years'_War) and further increased its influence during the reign of [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV). Under his rule, the nation built Europe's strongest army, fought a series of wars, and experienced artistic and scientific flourishing.
The [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution) of 1789 overthrew the [ancien régime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancien_régime) and produced the [Declaration of the Rights of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_the_Rights_of_Man_and_of_the_Citizen), which expresses the nation's ideals to this day. France reached its political and military zenith in the early 19th century under [Napoleon Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon), subjugating much of continental Europe and establishing the [First French Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_French_Empire). ### Colonial empire

The discredited Bourbon dynasty was overthrown by the [July Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_Revolution) of 1830, which established the constitutional [July Monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_Monarchy); French troops began the [conquest of Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_conquest_of_Algeria). Unrest led to the [French Revolution of 1848](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution_of_1848) and the end of the July Monarchy. The abolition of slavery and the introduction of male universal suffrage was re-enacted in 1848. In 1852, president of the French Republic, [Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III), Napoleon I's nephew, was proclaimed emperor of the [Second Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_French_Empire), as Napoleon III. He multiplied French interventions abroad, especially in [Crimea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_French_intervention_in_Mexico) and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Italian_War_of_Independence). Napoleon III was unseated following defeat in the [Franco-Prussian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) of 1870, and his regime was replaced by the [Third Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Third_Republic). By 1875, the French conquest of Algeria was complete, with approximately 825,000 Algerians killed from famine, disease, and violence.[[63]](#cite_note-Kiernan2007-74) France suffered an estimated 10,000 killed and 35,000 wounded across all colonial campaigns.[[47]](#cite_note-c-58) A few thousand died in Mexico or [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_conquest_of_Vietnam), but the vast majority perished in Algeria. Disease claimed an even heavier toll; one estimate puts total French and [Foreign Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Foreign_Legion) deaths from battle and disease for the entire 19th century at 110,000.[[47]](#cite_note-c-58)[French colonial empires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire):
  First
  Second
France had [colonial possessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire) since the beginning of the 17th century, but in the 19th and 20th centuries its empire extended significantly and became [the second-largest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires) behind the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire).[[64]](#cite_note-Lexington_Books-2005-75) Including metropolitan France, the total area reached almost 13 million square kilometres in the 1920s and 1930s, 9% of the world's land. Known as the [Belle Époque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belle_Époque), the turn of the century was characterised by optimism, regional peace, economic prosperity and technological, scientific and cultural innovations. In 1905, [state secularism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secular_state) was [officially established](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1905_French_law_on_the_Separation_of_the_Churches_and_the_State).[[65]](#cite_note-76)

### Early to mid-20th century (1914–1946)

Main article: [History of France (1900–present)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_France_(1900–present))French [Poilus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poilu) posing with their war-torn flag in 1917, during World War I
During World War I, France played a [decisive role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Army_in_World_War_I) in defeating the [Central Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Powers) as part of the [Triple Entente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_Entente), while participating in the majority of the war's major battles fought on the Western Front.[[66]](#cite_note-77) A rich industrial area in the north was occupied. France and the [Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_I) emerged victorious against the [Central Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Powers) at tremendous human cost. It left 1.4 million French soldiers dead, 4% of its population.[[67]](#cite_note-78)[[68]](#cite_note-79) In addition, France suffered 4,266,000 wounded.[[47]](#cite_note-c-58) Interwar was marked by [intense international tensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Events_preceding_World_War_II_in_Europe) and social reforms introduced by the [Popular Front government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Front_(France)) (e.g., [annual leave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annual_leave), [eight-hour workdays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-hour_day), [women in government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_government)).
In 1940, France was [invaded and quickly defeated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_France) by [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany). France was divided into a [German occupation zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_military_administration_in_occupied_France_during_World_War_II) in the north, an [Italian occupation zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_occupation_of_France) and an unoccupied territory, the rest of France, which consisted of southern France and the French empire. The [Vichy government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France), an authoritarian regime collaborating with Germany, ruled the unoccupied territory. [Free France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_France), the government-in-exile led by [Charles de Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle), was set up in London.[[69]](#cite_note-80)
From 1942 to 1944, about 160,000 French citizens, including around [75,000 Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust_in_France),[[70]](#cite_note-81) were deported to [death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extermination_camp) and [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment).[[71]](#cite_note-82) On 6 June 1944, the Allies [invaded Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Overlord), and in August they [invaded Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Dragoon). The Allies and [French Resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Resistance) emerged victorious, and French sovereignty was restored with the [Provisional Government of the French Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Government_of_the_French_Republic) (GPRF). This interim government, established by de Gaulle, continued to [wage war against Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Allied_invasion_of_Germany) and to [purge collaborators from office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Épuration_légale). It made important reforms e.g. suffrage extended to women and the creation of a [social security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_security_in_France) system.

## Politics

Main article: [Politics of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_France)
France is a [representative democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representative_democracy) organised as a unitary [semi-presidential republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-presidential_republic).[[117]](#cite_note-128) Democratic traditions and values are deeply rooted in French culture, identity and politics.[[118]](#cite_note-EncyclopediaBritannica-129) The [Constitution of the Fifth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_France) was approved by [referendum in 1958](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958_French_constitutional_referendum), establishing a framework consisting of executive, legislative and judicial branches.[[119]](#cite_note-130) It sought to address the instability of the Third and Fourth Republics by combining elements of both the parliamentary and presidential systems, while greatly strengthening the authority of the executive relative to the legislature.[[118]](#cite_note-EncyclopediaBritannica-129)

The executive branch has two leaders. The [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France), who is [Emmanuel Macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron) since 2017, is the [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state), elected directly by [universal adult suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_suffrage) for a five-year term.[[120]](#cite_note-131) The [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_France), who is [Sébastien Lecornu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sébastien_Lecornu) since 2025, is the [head of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government), appointed by the president to lead the government. The president has the power to dissolve [parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Parliament) or circumvent it by submitting referendums directly to the people; the president also appoints judges and civil servants, negotiates and ratifies international agreements, and serves as [commander-in-chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander-in-chief) of the [French Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Armed_Forces). The prime minister determines public policy and oversees the civil service, with an emphasis on domestic matters.[[121]](#cite_note-132) In the [2022 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_French_presidential_election), Macron was re-elected.[[122]](#cite_note-133) Two months later in the [legislative elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_French_legislative_election), Macron lost his parliamentary majority and had to form a [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government).[[123]](#cite_note-134)[Palais Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Bourbon) is the meeting place of the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(France)), the lower legislative chamber of the [French Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Parliament).
The legislature consists of the French Parliament, a [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameralism) body made up of a [lower house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_house), the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(France)), and an [upper house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_house), the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_(France)).[[124]](#cite_note-135) Legislators in the National Assembly, known as [députés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_(France)), represent local constituencies and are [directly elected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_election) for five-year terms.[[125]](#cite_note-136) The Assembly has the power to dismiss the government by majority vote. Senators are chosen by an [electoral college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_college) for six-year terms, with half the seats submitted to election every three years.[[126]](#cite_note-137) The Senate's legislative powers are limited; in the event of disagreement between the two chambers, the National Assembly has the final say.[[127]](#cite_note-138) The parliament is responsible for determining the rules and principles concerning most areas of law, political amnesty, and fiscal policy; however, the government may draft specific details concerning most laws.
From World War II until 2017, French politics was dominated by two politically opposed groupings: one left-wing, the [French Section of the Workers' International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Section_of_the_Workers'_International), which was succeeded by the [Socialist Party](https://en.", "relevance": ["cited in the draft"], "source_chars": 445564, "start": 94696, "title": "France - Wikipedia", "url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France"}
